intended: In cases one and three the shorter cycle time was recorded before the coolant was switched: 29 March precedes 4 May, and 30 September precedes 5 October. Half the evidence therefore describes runs that had already sped up when the treatment was introduced, so it cannot be evidence for the treatment. The two remaining cases are not enough on their own.
reported: Two of the four runs are measured before the coolant was switched: run one 'switched 4 May' but 'ran 6 minutes shorter by 29 March', and run three 'switched 5 October' but shorter 'by 30 September'. The improvement in those cases predates the intervention, so the dates run backwards.

intended: The mid-passage line tallies the timings over the runs that stayed on the issued route, and the clause beside it records that about a sixth of each depot's runs left the issued route. The claim is about delivery time on the runs the routing change was rolled out to, so the population is every run dispatched and the minute figures describe roughly five sixths of it. A run leaves the issued route when it meets a blockage or a diversion, which is exactly what makes a run come in long, so an average taken over the runs that stayed on it sits below the figure for all runs dispatched, and the reductions of 8, 5, 9 and 6 minutes are consistent with no reduction at all. Every case is vans out of Kettleby Wharf in February under dispatcher Verhoeven, so one and the same exclusion sits under all four groups at once.
reported: The outcome is measured on a self-selected subset: "Timings cover the runs that stayed on the issued route, and about a sixth of each depot's runs left the issued route." The excluded sixth is exactly the set most likely to have run long, and it is compared against "the same runs a month earlier," i.e. the full unfiltered population.

reported: The measured population is narrower than the claim: 'Timings cover the runs that stayed on the issued route', while 'about a sixth of each depot's runs left the issued route' and are therefore excluded. The runs most likely to abandon a new route are the ones where it went badly, so the 5-9 minute saving is computed on a filtered subset rather than on the routing change's actual effect.

intended: All four plots sit on one reserve, with one species in one spring under one warden, so the single fact stated mid-passage covers every case at once: prey abundance on the surrounding farmland doubled from the previous year, which is an alternative cause of higher fledgling counts. The scope clause beside that fact puts every box at the farmland edge, within the birds' foraging range, so the food surge reaches every brood that was counted. Each plot is measured against the same reserve a year earlier rather than against an unboxed wood in the same spring, so nothing in the evidence separates the boxes from the prey peak. The population and completeness clauses in the same line leave the tally covering the whole set of installed boxes, so they add no second defect.
reported: A named alternative cause reaches every plot: "Prey abundance on the surrounding farmland doubled from the previous year" and "every box stood at the farmland edge, within the birds' foraging range", so the extra 9-16 fledglings at Hollowmere could be the doubled food supply rather than the boxes.

intended: The absence figures are tallied over "the pupils on the revised timetable throughout", while the same line records that "about a fifth of each cohort spent weeks on the old timetable". The claim is about absence in the cohorts that moved to the revised timetable, and that population includes the pupils who spent weeks back on the old schedule. Those pupils are the part of each cohort the change sat least firmly on, and their absence is precisely what the figures leave out, so the 4 to 7 percent falls are consistent with cohort absence not having moved at all. All four cases are Year 9 at Brackhill Academy in one autumn term, so the same exclusion applies identically in every case and no case corrects another.

intended: The mid-passage line tallies the particulate figures over the runs with the upgraded filter in service, and the clause beside it records that a quarter of each stack's runs were made with the filter bypassed. The claim is about the upgrade lowering particulate at the stack across its monitored period, so the population is every scheduled run at that stack and the figures describe three quarters of them. Bypass goes in under heavy load and upset conditions, which are the runs carrying the dirtiest gas, so a stack can post a lower figure over its in-service runs with its particulate across the period unchanged. All four kilns sit at Kestrel in Q1 and the same quarter of runs sits outside the figures at each, so no case in the log covers the runs the others leave out.
reported: The reported 8-14 percent reductions come from a hand-picked slice of runs: "The figures cover the runs with the upgraded filter in service, and a quarter of each stack's runs were made with the filter bypassed" - so the 25 percent of post-upgrade runs with the filter out of circuit are dropped from the post figures while the earlier quarter's comparison presumably includes all runs. That is a narrower population than the claim, and it selects the runs most favourable to the upgrade.
